blocks.text: **The problem.** Given two integer arrays `a` and `b`, return every value that appears in **both**. Each value in the result must be **unique**, and the result may be in any order.

blocks.alt: a = [4, 9, 5] and b = [9, 4, 9, 8, 4]. The values 4 and 9 appear in both arrays, so the intersection is [4, 9].

blocks.text: Example

blocks.code:
Input:  a = [1, 2, 2, 1], b = [2, 2]
Output: [2]

Input:  a = [4, 9, 5], b = [9, 4, 9, 8, 4]
Output: [4, 9]     ([9, 4] is also accepted)

blocks.text: Understanding the problem
Two details matter. First, **duplicates collapse**: 2 appears twice in each array of the first example, but the answer lists it once. Second, **order doesn't matter**, which leaves us free to sort.
Brute force
For every value of `a`, scan all of `b` to see whether it's there, skipping values already added.
`b.includes(x)` is itself a loop, so this is **O(n × m)**.
Approach 1: a hash set
Put every value of `a` into a set. Then walk `b`, and whenever a value is in the set, add it to the answer and remove it from the set (so it can't be added twice).
Each lookup is O(1) on average, so this is **O(n + m) time**, using **O(n) extra space** for the set. It's the go-to answer when the arrays are unsorted.
Approach 2: sort, then walk both arrays
If the arrays are sorted — or you're asked to avoid the extra space of a set — sort both and walk them together with one pointer each:

items: If `a[i] < b[j]`, the value `a[i]` can't be in `b` any more (everything ahead in `b` is bigger), so move `i`.
If `a[i] > b[j]`, by the same reasoning move `j`.
If they're equal, the value is in both: record it (unless it was just recorded) and move both pointers.

blocks.alt: Walking the sorted arrays a = [4, 5, 9] and b = [4, 4, 8, 9, 9] together. Equal fronts are recorded; otherwise the pointer on the smaller value moves.

Complexity

blocks.alt: Brute force: O(n × m) time. Hash set: O(n + m) time and O(n) space. Sort and walk: O(n log n + m log m) time.

blocks.text: Pick the **hash set** for speed on unsorted input; pick **sort and walk** when the inputs are already sorted (then it's just O(n + m)) or when memory is tight.

blocks.text: Where this idea shows up again

A common follow-up, "Intersection of Two Arrays II", keeps duplicates: a value should appear as many times as it appears in **both** arrays. Just remove the uniqueness check — each equal pair of fronts is one more match. Walking sorted arrays together also powers **Union of two sorted arrays**, the next problem.
